source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding (JEP:LMC 30, 14-27; author preprint)
finding: Restates the progress monitoring rule in explicit arithmetic. A move meets the criterion of satisfactory progress if it closes at least (distance left) divided by (moves left). If no move meets it, 'criterion failure' happens and the solver relaxes the demand to maximise, which opens up non-maximal moves.
numbers: Nine-dot start: 9 dots / 4 lines = criterion of 2.25 dots on the first line, so a 3-dot line passes. Six-coin ring version: 2 coins short in 3 moves = 0.67 per move, so first move must put 5 coins on the ring.
quote: individuals evaluate potential moves against a criterion of satisfactory progress
limits: Criterion is inferred by the authors from move statistics, not measured directly. Needs a fixed move limit and a countable progress variable.
agent_relevance: This is a ready formula for a code-side stall detector: progress needed per step = gap / steps left. Needs a countable gap, which many LLM tasks lack.

source: Chronicle et al. (2004) Experiment 1, six-coin problem, ring goal vs abstract goal
finding: A fine quantitative prediction held. Hill-climbing predicts which move is correct about 11% of the time at move 1, 33% at move 2, 100% at move 3. Observed values matched almost exactly. Solving was far above chance, so people were not guessing.
numbers: N=40 (19 analysed in Ring). 6/19 (32%) solved in 10 min. 177 first moves, 20 correct (11.3% vs 11% predicted). 6 of 20 correct first moves followed by correct second (30% vs 33%); 6/6 then correct third. Mean coins on ring after move 1 = 4.42 vs chance 4.08, t(18)=3.02, p<.01. Chance solution rate .00015 per attempt.
limits: Only 19 per cell. Fit was to a model with free parameters (lookahead mix). Authors note power for the abstract condition was only .38.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a simple 'maximise visible progress' policy explains where a solver gets stuck. LLM agents likely do the same, so a progress counter will mostly say 'fine' right up to the dead end.

source: Chronicle et al. (2004) Experiment 1, abstract-goal condition (two-group solution)
finding: When the goal was only stated abstractly, most people still pictured a ring and so still hill-climbed toward it. The alternative (two-group) solution was found no more often than chance. Solvers infer goal properties and use them as the progress test.
numbers: n=19. 74% inferred a ring goal. 5/19 (26%) found two-group solution vs about 2.2 expected by chance (not significant, power .38). Only 6/124 final states (4.8%) separated the coins vs 16.1% in the full state space, chi2=11.68.
limits: Low power. The authors admit some successes may be random. Also fits a plain fixation story.
agent_relevance: The progress measure is only as good as the goal the agent inferred. If the agent mis-infers the goal, its progress signal drives it the wrong way. Restate the goal and check it before trusting any progress number.

source: Chronicle et al. (2004) Experiment 2, partial-ring vs straight-line start
finding: Changing only the start layout, so that a ring goal looked less natural, raised solution of the two-move task. This isolates the goal-conception effect. It discriminates against a pure 'avoid breaking up a good figure' account.
numbers: N=54 school students, 3 min. Partial-ring 4/27 (15%) vs straight-line 11/27 (41%) solved, chi2(1,54)=4.52, p<.05. Chance solutions 2.1 (straight-line): 11 observed, binomial p<.001. Partial-ring 4 vs 2.8 chance, n.s.
limits: Chance level estimated from attempt rates in a different experiment because attempts were not logged. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Priming a wrong goal picture in the prompt makes the true answer harder to reach by 26 points here. Keep goal wording neutral until a check fails.

source: Chronicle et al. (2004) Experiment 3, goal-example manipulation
finding: Showing the correct goal raised success sharply. Showing the competing (ring) goal did not help and slowed the first discovery. A concrete goal makes the progress test sharp.
numbers: N=42. Two-group solution found by 3/11 (27%) Abstract, 3/11 (27%) Ring example, 8/9 (89%) Two-group example, 10/11 (91%) Both examples; chi2(3,42)=16.84. Two-group example sped up attempts F(1,20)=18.08, p<.001. Ring example slowed them F(1,20)=6.92, p<.02.
limits: Cell sizes 9 to 11. Participants who saw the answer shape can solve by pattern matching, which is not insight.
agent_relevance: A target-state description is the single strongest lever on whether progress tracking points the right way. Moving from 27% to about 90% with a concrete goal is the largest effect seen in this subfield.

source: Chronicle et al. (2004) Experiment 4, six-coin vs ten-coin (triangle) problem
finding: The same hill-climbing move choice appeared in a classic insight problem and a transformation problem. Most correct ten-coin solutions were consistent with hill-climbing, not with a sudden change. Supports 'one mechanism' over 'insight is a special process'. Also shows solution recoding: solutions were hard to reproduce afterwards.
numbers: N=50 (48 usable). Solved within 5 min: six-coin 10 (20.8%) vs ten-coin 36 (75%); solve at first attempt 0% vs 19%, Wilcoxon z=2.65-2.67, p=.008. First ten-coin moves consistent with hill-climbing 69% vs 17% chance (chi2(1,42)=77.61). Of classifiable ten-coin solutions, 56% fit hill-climbing, 24% fit the rotational (insight) pattern. Exp 1: only 2/6 ring-solvers could reproduce the solution at once.
limits: Move-type classification is by the authors. 'Consistent with' is weaker than 'caused by'. Does not test representational change directly.
agent_relevance: Hints that human solvers often reach the answer by the same stepwise rule even for 'insight' items. A step-wise progress monitor is not wasted on such tasks.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (JEP:LMC 29, 1017-1027; author preprint)
finding: The only head-to-head test of progress monitoring vs representational change in an unlimited-move task (car park / Rush Hour). Progress monitoring predicts no effect of changing the practice sequence or rotating the board; representational change predicts a gain. A gain appeared. The author concludes both get some support but representational change fits better.
numbers: N=39 undergraduates (13 per condition: Normal, Rotated, Easy). 31 solved without hint. Solvers: Normal 7/13 (54%), Rotated 12/13, Easy 12/13 (collapsed 24/26, 92%); Fisher exact p=.01. Erroneous clicks fewer in Rotated/Easy, U=76, p<.01. Moves and time to solution among solvers did not differ (p>.05).
limits: Tiny sample. Only one problem. Progress monitoring needs a move limit, so the unlimited-move design stretches the theory (Jones says criterion failure is never reached by definition). Table 3 in the preprint is partly garbled in text extraction; Normal=7/13 solvers is read from totals.
agent_relevance: Evidence for choosing triggers: a manipulation that does not change distance-to-goal still changed solving. A pure counter of progress would miss it. Keep representation-changing operators available even when the counter says 'on track'.

source: Jones (2003), impasse and eye-movement analysis
finding: Impasse was defined from the player's own fixation times, not a fixed cut-off. All solvers had an impasse before the key move. Non-solvers who tried the key move did not get the benefit because they did not link it to the right area of the board. Time spent in impasse (not count of impasses) matched progress monitoring's predicted lookahead mix.
numbers: 37 analysable: 30 solvers (all had impasse before the taxi move, 5 immediately before), 7 non-solvers. Taxi move longer than moves before or after, F(2,58)=5.40, p<.01. Fixations on the key right-hand area: solvers 24% vs non-solvers 9%, F(1,39)=6.50, p<.05. MacGregor et al lookahead mix used for prediction: 32% / 32% / 36% for lookahead 1/2/3.
limits: Eight non-solvers. Individual-threshold impasse definition is a choice. Lookahead assignment depends on which of four definitions of 'majority' is used.
agent_relevance: A usable impasse definition: a pause or repeat that is long relative to this solver's own baseline, not a fixed number. For an agent, relative to its own median step length or token count.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci proceedings)
finding: Rival account of nine-dot difficulty, built from the MacGregor data: people avoid turning on a non-dot point and avoid crossing lines. Training on these two actions beat training on the opposite habits. Hindering training did not make things worse than control (floor effect).
numbers: N=90 undergraduates, 30 per group. First insight problem solved: facilitating 19/30 (63%), hindering 8/30 (27%), no training 11/30 (37%); chi2(2,N=90)=8.836, p<.05. Facilitating vs no training chi2(1,60)=4.267; hindering vs no training n.s. Facilitating mean 116 s vs 188 and 185 s, F(2,87)=5.873. Those who completed training correctly: 17/19 (89%) solved vs 2/11 (18%).
limits: Non-random split inside the facilitating group (completers vs non-completers). 4-minute limit. Floor effect on the hindering side. Not a test of lookahead.
agent_relevance: Practice on the specific blocked move class works (63% vs 37%), much more than telling the solver the rule. Suggests a small bank of worked 'break the habit' examples inside the scaffold rather than generic advice.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2001), summary of earlier hint and training studies on the nine-dot problem
finding: Telling people they may go outside the square helped only when combined with hints that gave away part of the answer. Standard solution rate is under 5% in minutes. Changing the shape or giving training with lines outside the figure helped. This is why a simple 'stay inside the box' constraint is not the whole story.
numbers: Base rate under 5% (Lung and Dominowski 1985; MacGregor et al 2001). Burnham and Davis 1969 and Weisberg and Alba 1981 found the 'go outside' instruction alone did not help.
quote: the instruction only worked if combined with other hints that gave away part of the solution
limits: Second-hand report of old studies. Exact numbers not given here.
agent_relevance: Naming the hidden constraint alone does not unblock. The scaffold should offer a concrete move to try, not a statement of the rule.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter, Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem (Memory and Cognition 38, 883-892)
finding: First direct test of the lookahead mechanism. Spatial working memory capacity (a stand-in for lookahead depth) predicted drawing outside the grid and solving a hint-aided version. Verbal working memory did not. This supports the information-processing model, against the view that insight needs no planning.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=51-52, standard problem, 10 min): only 7 (14%) drew outside the grid, 6 of those from the high spatial WM group, chi2(1,51)=4.15, p=.04; verbal WM n.s. 5/51 (about 10%) solved. Exp 2 (N=54, training plus hint): 25/54 (46%) solved; 19 of 25 solvers in high spatial WM group, chi2(1,54)=12.59, p<.001; verbal WM split 12 vs 13. Spatial WM recall odds ratio 1.16 per point, p=.005. Solvers SSPAN 31.72 vs non-solvers 24.42, t(52)=3.51.
limits: Standard problem solve rate (10%) too low for strong tests. Exp 2 used hints and training, so it is a modified task. Median splits. Correlational. Spatial WM may also index general ability.
agent_relevance: The strongest independent support for the lookahead part. Lookahead depth predicts stall detection and escape. For an LLM that means budget for explicit forward simulation of the remaining steps before declaring a path viable.

source: Chein et al. (2010) Experiment 3, feeling-of-warmth ratings on the nine-dot problem
finding: Replicates the Metcalfe and Wiebe pattern for the nine-dot problem. Self-rated closeness to solution stayed flat for minutes, then jumped only 15 seconds before the solution. Non-solvers stayed flat. So solvers cannot feel progress until just before the end.
numbers: N=25 (12 solved, 48%; mean 221 s). Group x time interaction F(1,20)=20.60, p<.001. Solvers vs non-solvers differ only at 15 s (t(20)=2.96, p=.007) and 0 s (t(15)=7.27, p<.001). Flat for about 3.5 min on average.
limits: Small N, only 5 solvers at the final time point. Verbal reports while solving may alter the process. Hint-aided version.
agent_relevance: Self-reported progress is a poor early signal on this class of problem. Any LLM 'how close are you' estimate should be treated as unreliable until validated against outcomes.

source: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, as reported in Chein et al. (2010)
finding: Reported second-hand. Warmth ratings rose gradually on routine problems and jumped suddenly just before solution on insight problems. This is the classic result that makes progress estimates suspect for insight.
numbers: No figures reported in the source I read.
limits: Not opened directly. Graf et al. (2023) say later studies found both sudden and incremental patterns, so the dichotomy is not clean.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a flat progress curve as proof of being lost, and do not treat a smooth one as proof of being right.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt, Szathmary (2017; Psychological Research 81, 925-938) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization
finding: A clean test of the 'combined account'. Relaxing constraints alone did nothing for solving. Adding a search criterion (maximise intersections, each line exactly four) is what raised solving. Both parts are needed.
numbers: N=120 (4 groups of 30; 116 analysed). Hint given at 5 min, 15 min total. Solvers/group: control 3/30 (10%), lines hint 2/29 (7%), lines+intersections 6/28 (21%), maximization 21/29 (72%). MG vs CG chi2(1,59)=23.80, phi=.64, p<.0001; LG vs MG phi=.67; IG vs MG phi=.51; no other pair differs. Logistic model classified 87.8% correctly.
limits: One problem (ten-penny). Hint after 5 min conflates timing. Four participants solved before the hint and were dropped. Maximization hint is also nearly a partial answer.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that the scaffold should pair 'change representation' with 'give a concrete progress criterion'. A relaxed constraint without a way to score moves is worth about nothing (7% vs 10% control).

source: Oellinger et al. (2017), solvers vs non-solvers
finding: Successful solvers varied their attempts more, repeated less, tried fewer total attempts, and were more likely to use intersections early. Variation and maximization scores were the most useful behavioural predictors. Gives cheap counters for stall detection.
numbers: 32 solvers and 84 non-solvers. Variation rate .59 (SD .24) solvers vs .43 (SD .24), t(114)=3.10, d=.67. Attempts 8.41 (SD 2.76) vs 10.93 (SD 4.91), t(114)=2.74, d=.62. Intersections used before hint: 47% of solvers vs 26% of non-solvers, chi2(1,116)=4.56, phi=.20. Before the hint, 18/30 (60%) of controls used only the penny strategy; after 5 min 10/30 (33%).
limits: Variation rate is a post hoc score defined by the authors. Medium effects, one task. Solvers were also more successful at generating attempts so reverse causation is possible.
agent_relevance: Concrete stall counters: repeat rate across attempts (share of attempts with the same strategy as the last one), and strategy-class change. Low variation across attempts is the signal; the effect is medium (d about .6).

source: Oellinger, Jones, Knoblich (2014) The dynamics of search, impasse, and representational change provide a coherent explanation of difficulty in the nine-dot problem (Psychological Research 78, 266-275); described in Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: As reported by the 2017 paper and a search abstract: a staged account. Early on solvers maximise dots (as MacGregor says). After repeated failures, solvers who change the representation get a larger search space which again needs heuristics. Hints of increasing strength sped up representational change and raised solving.
numbers: Three hint conditions of increasing strength vs control; exact rates not read.
limits: Not opened, only the summary paragraph in a later paper and a search abstract. Rates unknown.
agent_relevance: Argues the two theories are sequential, not rivals: progress monitoring early, representation change at the impasse, search again after. A good template for state order S-search then S6 impasse then re-search.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci, Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis (J. Intelligence 11, 86)
finding: Reanalysis of matchstick eye-tracking data. Ordinary ANOVA missed abrupt representational change; non-linear models and change-point analysis found it. The authors also review studies and report both sudden and incremental solution patterns in different studies and tasks. Explicit hints changed the dynamics.
numbers: Source text states 'both incremental and sudden solution patterns were found' in Cushen and Wiley 2012, Danek et al. 2020 and Novick and Sherman 2003, and only incremental in Durso et al. 1994. Task phases split into ten relative time bins.
limits: Reanalysis of one prior eye-tracking dataset (Bilalic et al. 2019). Matchstick arithmetic only. I did not extract sample size.
agent_relevance: Supports building the impasse detector on change points in a time series of cheap measures, not on thresholded averages. Averaged curves hide sudden shifts.

source: Fedor, Zachar, Szilagyi, Oellinger, de Vladar, Szathmary (2017) Cognitive architecture with evolutionary dynamics solves insight problem (Frontiers in Psychology 8, 427)
finding: A neural model of the four-tree problem. It does not model impasse itself but names two behavioural correlates of impasse used in the literature: inactivity and repeated candidate solutions. The model shows a 'beginner's luck' effect: primed but not pretrained was best, and reduced capacity lowered performance.
numbers: Model was benchmarked on human data from Kershaw et al. (2013). Exact solution-rate figures not extracted.
quote: Repeated candidate solutions are the two behavioral associates of impasse.
limits: Computational model on one problem; not a test of progress monitoring. I read the discussion on impasse, not every result table.
agent_relevance: Gives a minimal behavioural definition of impasse that code can compute: long idle time or a repeated candidate. Both are cheap on an LLM trace (token gap, duplicate answer).

source: Spiridonov, Loginov, Ivanchei, Kurgansky (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving: the nine-dot case (Frontiers in Psychology 10, 2)
finding: Tested whether learning a motor part of the solution transfers. Experiment 3 expected benefit from implicit motor learning of a fraction of the answer; it did not appear. Authors tie the 'long horizon' of off-line planning to lookahead and to Chein's spatial memory link, and note the planning stays inside the perceptual frame.
numbers: Exact solution rates not extracted from this read; the text reports that the expected benefit 'did not confirm' in Experiment 3.
limits: Read the introduction and discussion, not the full results. Motor-learning angle is only indirectly about progress monitoring.
agent_relevance: Another null for 'practise part of the answer in the same form': showing a fragment of the move did not help, in line with the nine-dot hint literature.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov, Ardislamov (2025) Sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra (Frontiers, open access; conceptual extended replication)
finding: Failed conceptual replication of the claim that acting on materials with the hands helps insight. Three experiment series did not reproduce the interactivity benefit. Movement helped with chunk decomposition not at all and interfered with relaxing high-level constraints.
numbers: Exp 1 N=105: interactive assembled sticks vs static sticks solved problems A/B/C/D 0.91/0.87/0.59/0.67 vs 0.94/0.80/0.59/0.69. Exp 2 N=88; Exp 3 N=74. Bayesian regression: condition effect on problem C median 0.07 log-odds, 95% CrI (-0.73, 0.82), inconclusive either way.
limits: Small cells (20-25 in Exp 2 and 3). Success rates high at baseline (about 86%), ceiling. Bayesian results are 'uncertain', not proof of no effect. About matchsticks, not progress monitoring.
agent_relevance: A reminder that popular insight interventions often fail to replicate. Our scaffold's operators should each be tested on our own tasks before being trusted.

source: Kobe University Q-learning study (2023) Q-learning model of insight problem solving and effects of learning traits on creativity (Frontiers, open access)
finding: Eight-coin and nine-dot problems, 325 students. Success on one task predicted success on the other, and a reinforcement-learning fit showed that people who reacted positively to negative outcomes did better. Suggests individual differences in how failure feedback is used, which is the signal progress monitoring relies on.
numbers: N=325 analysed (364 recruited; 7 incomplete, 32 had met a task before). Loss aversion lambda effect on 8-coin about -0.62 to -0.63 (p<.05) in Table 3; success on 9-dot positively predicted 8-coin success and vice versa.
limits: Only partly read. Individual-difference fits to a two-armed bandit task; indirect link to insight. Success rates not extracted.
agent_relevance: Humans differ in how they use negative feedback. An agent should have a fixed rule for how a failed check changes the next step, not vary it by mood of the generation.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod, Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of nine-dot and related problems (JEP:LMC 27, 176-201), as described in Chronicle 2004, Jones 2003, Kershaw and Ohlsson 2001, Oellinger 2017
finding: The founding paper was not available as full text (paywalled). Four opened papers describe it the same way: maximise dots per line, check the ratio of dots left to lines left, look ahead 1 to 4 lines, and try non-maximal lines when criterion failure happens. Its model predicted differences in solution rate between many nine-dot variants. A line drawn diagonally inside the square made the task easier than a line drawn out to a non-dot point.
numbers: As cited: lookahead mix 32% / 32% / 36% for lookahead 1 / 2 / 3 (Jones 2003). Standard nine-dot solve rate under 5% (Kershaw and Ohlsson 2001).
limits: Primary source not read. All numbers second-hand. Fits were to its own data.
agent_relevance: The theory's testable core is the claim that failure comes from a progress-satisfying rule, not from a shape constraint. Our detector design should follow the four opened descriptions, and the original should be checked when full text is available.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor, Chronicle (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving (JEP:LMC 28, 791-799), described in Jones 2003 and Chronicle 2004
finding: Eight-coin problem. The problem was solved faster when no starting move gave a coin touching three others than when several did. Fits the claim that moves that satisfy the progress criterion trap solvers.
numbers: No figures in the sources I read.
limits: Not opened. Described in Jones 2003 and Chronicle 2004 only.
agent_relevance: Another way to induce a stall: a problem with many locally attractive moves. Check an agent's step choice against the count of such moves.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Faber, Knoblich (2013) Cognitive mechanisms of insight: heuristics and representational change in the eight-coin problem (JEP:LMC 39, 931-939), cited in Spiridonov et al. 2019
finding: Cited as a combined account for the eight-coin task: heuristic search plus representational change. Only the citation was seen.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. Not even an abstract this session.
agent_relevance: A target for a later pass; it is the direct combined-account test on the problem Ormerod et al. created.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks, as summarised in a search result
finding: Search result summary: a strong influence of representational change on solution rates, and minimal influence of heuristics, in matchstick arithmetic. Opposite direction to the nine-dot results, so the weight of each mechanism depends on the task.
numbers: None read.
limits: Only a repository abstract seen. The PDF did not download.
agent_relevance: Task-type moderator: in single-step tasks representation matters most, in multi-step tasks progress heuristics do. A stall detector should be switched on only for multi-step tasks.

source: Mavi, Jaroria, Sun (2025) Self-evaluating LLMs for multi-step tasks: stepwise confidence estimation for failure detection (NeurIPS 2025 multi-turn workshop; arXiv 2511.07364)
finding: Scoring every step beat scoring only the final answer for catching errors in multi-step LLM work, especially in dialogue. A trained regression scorer was best. Verbalised self-reports of confidence were close to useless. A step-level process reward model also did poorly on this task.
numbers: Llama-3.2-11B agent; GSM8K (avg 5.1 steps) and CoQA (avg 13.5 steps). Best methods reach AUC-ROC about .9 with false positive rate under one third at recall .9. Self-verbalised confidence AUC .556 (response) and .546 (step) on GSM8K; .502 and .624 on CoQA. Regression GSM8K .843 to .907; CoQA .689 to .952. Self-certainty CoQA .523 to .849 per step but GSM8K .649 to .395. In 60/879 GSM8K cases the answer was right but a step was wrong.
limits: Needs training data for the regression scorer. Small 11B agent. Labels are correctness of a step, not progress. Workshop paper, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: The nearest LLM analogue of a progress estimator. Verbalised confidence is near chance; a trained scorer on hidden states or a regression head works. Prefer checks computed by code, and use a learned scorer only if it is validated on our own traces.

source: Sophia self-loop steering paper (2026) Can we break LLMs out of self-loops? Fine-grained reasoning control with activation steering (arXiv 2607.18100), abstract page only
finding: Reports that failed reasoning trajectories get stuck in self-loops until the token budget runs out. A controller detects loops online from latent-state transitions and applies a steering vector. Claims better accuracy and token efficiency.
numbers: None on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; needs activation access, so not usable for a black-box scaffold. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Confirms the stuck-in-a-loop failure exists in LLMs, matching the human 'repeated candidate solution' impasse sign. Black-box version: detect duplicate steps in text.

source: Reasoning path deviation monitoring (2026) Mitigating overthinking in large reasoning language models via reasoning path deviation monitoring (arXiv 2603.14251), abstract page only
finding: A path deviation index counts high-entropy transition tokens and stops a reasoning trace early when it signals drift. Claims the best gain over plain chain of thought among early-exit methods.
numbers: None on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Needs token entropies, so white-box or log-prob access.
agent_relevance: A cheap progress proxy from the decoder, not from the model's own claims. A candidate trigger if log-probs are available.

source: ProgRouter (2026) Online progress-guided orchestration for multi-agent LLM workflows (arXiv 2608.25992), abstract page only
finding: Estimates task progress online from subtask completion, progress trend and workflow state quality, then routes each step to a model. Claims lower cost with maintained quality on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500 and ASQA.
numbers: No figures on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Progress is a learned predictor, not an interpretable criterion.
agent_relevance: Industry version of a progress estimator that uses subtask completion and trend. Matches the human 'distance to goal vs steps left' idea.

source: Cross-source synthesis: what discriminates progress monitoring from representational change
finding: Opened sources agree on a ladder. (1) Move-statistics experiments show stepwise maximisation of visible progress (Chronicle 2004: 11.3% vs 11% predicted). (2) Manipulations that leave distance-to-goal unchanged still change solving (Jones 2003: 54% vs 92%). (3) Constraint relaxation without a progress criterion fails (Oellinger 2017: 7% vs 10% control, then 72% with criterion). (4) Lookahead capacity predicts escape (Chein 2010). The accounts look sequential, not rival.
numbers: Figures as listed in b02, b07, b11, b14. No meta-analysis exists in the sources opened; the largest N for any single test of this theory was 325 (Q-learning study, indirect) and 120 (ten-penny); direct tests have 39 to 120 people.
limits: No large-sample replication of the criterion of satisfactory progress was found. Tasks are small spatial puzzles, mostly undergraduates in the UK, USA, Germany and Japan. No culture or expertise moderator was found in any opened source.
agent_relevance: For the schema: a code-side stall detector (progress below gap/steps-left, repeat rate high, long pause) is justified, but the escape action must change the representation AND supply a new progress criterion. Test both on our own tasks.
